specs.note: ASTM 2558 test protocol; with vermiculite panels (EO-VP1500)

rows: 2 ½" under base, 2 ½" in front

steps: Move it on its crate

It is front heavy and weighs 970 lb crated, so unpack it only beside its final spot. Use an Escalera or equivalent dolly with the upper strap just above the upper finishing lintel and the lower strap just under the metal front step; never lean it on its side or lift it by the front or door opening (use the casing or the lifting handles).
Install the counterweights

Feed the three cables over the pulleys through openings A and C, seat the counterweights on the blocking rods (right side: larger rear, smaller front, plate toward the back) and connect the cables to the door and firescreen. Then lift each weight off its rod and remove the rods.

Firescreen counterweight1 smaller, approx. 11 lb
Glass door counterweights2 bigger, approx. 35 lb each
  1. Feed the three counterweight cables through openings A and C and over the pulleys (left, right back, right front); let them hang toward the door.
  2. Make sure the pre-installed blocking rods are in position, then set each counterweight in its channel. Right side: the larger one in the rear channel, the smaller one in the front channel with its extended metal plate toward the back.
  3. Connect the three cables to the counterweights and tighten the nuts.
  4. Connect the hanging cables to the bottom of the door, left and right, and to the bottom of the firescreen at the front right.
  5. With pliers, remove the caps on the back of each blocking rod. Wearing gloves, pull the cable through opening A to lift the weight off its rod, remove the rod and gently let the weight hang. Repeat through opening C.
Don't try to lift the door at this point. Openings A and C get covered by cement board; they have no metal cover plates.
Unlock the door, fit the top cover

Check the firescreen cable runs centered on its pulley, remove the two transportation blocking brackets (¼" hex head screws), push in the door cover buttons and check the door. With both closed, fix the top finishing cover (two small self-tapping screws to the sides, five along the back edge) and recheck travel.
Bottom standoff & spark guard

Mandatory on any combustible floor: screw ¾" plywood to the sub-floor every 4-6" in a grid, assemble the standoff (eight large self-tapping screws), place it with the spark guard per Figure 8 and fasten with at least 1½" wood screws (3" into joists where possible).

On a non-combustible floor (surface and structure) the standoff is optional. On any combustible floor surface or structure it is mandatory, and the sub-floor must be reinforced to spread the load from the standoff legs.

  1. Cut ¾" plywood to the size of the fireplace enclosure and fix it to the sub-floor with wood screws every 4-6" in a grid.
  2. Assemble the bottom standoff shield to both supports with eight large self-tapping screws (provided).
  3. Position the standoff and the spark guard using Figure 8 (the silhouette includes the back and angled side standoffs).
  4. Screw the left and right sides, and the front and back of the inner sides, to the floor with at least 1½" wood screws (not provided); into the joists with 3" wood screws if possible.
  5. Set the fireplace on the standoff with its base aligned to it.

The spark guard sits 2½" under the fireplace base and 2½" under the hearth extension, centered on the opening, and covers the floor under the metal front step. A combustible raised platform needs a second spark guard (not provided): one below the hearth extension and platform, one below the fireplace, both centered.
Anchor it with the brackets

Fasten the casing to the floor: the small crate brackets without the standoff, or four anti-tip brackets and eight large self-tapping screws with it. Add two anti-tip brackets from the top of the casing to the back wall (eight large self-tapping screws).
Hearth extension

Non-combustible flooring (brick, tile, stone or slate) at least 67" wide × 24" deep, centered on the glass door opening. On a combustible floor it goes over thermal protection of at least R-Value 2.20, which sits over the spark guard.
Outside air (if used)

Left side only, 4" collar. FO-INT kit for runs of 10' or less, 5" duct for 20' or more; no more than 12' of vertical rise, and don't terminate within 5' of the chimney top or in an attic, crawl space or garage.
Chimney

ICC RIS 12" through 18" square framed openings with 2" to combustibles (no insulation): radiation shield RM-12RRS2 at each floor, mandatory roof top shield RM-12RTS, flashing, storm collar and rain cap. Terminate at least 3' above the roof penetration and 2' above anything within 10'.

1. Frame 18" square rough openings in floors, ceilings and roof (up to 18½", never smaller). Keep 2" or more to combustibles and don't fill it with insulation.
  2. Fit the first length on the fireplace flue adapter with the screws provided; add lengths lining up the seams and pre-punched holes, plus supports as required.
  3. At each floor, install a radiation shield (RM-12RRS2). In the United States, reinstall its ring below the cylinder using all the screws. Pitched ceiling: Cathedral Ceiling Radiation Shield RM-12RRSC or RM-12RRSCA.
  4. At the attic level, a radiation shield and a storm collar.
  5. At the roof, the mandatory roof top shield (RM-12RTS); set its two support brackets in the holes for the installation number that matches your roof pitch and flashing (Table 9).
  6. Vented flashing is required if the chimney is in a chase or enclosed to the roof; don't caulk its vents. The manual's text names RF-12RVF; its Table 9 lists vented flashing by roof pitch: RF-12RVF for 0/12, RF-12RVFA for 1/12 to 7/12 and RF-12RVFB for 8/12 to 12/12 (US only), and RF-12RCVF, RF-12RCVFA and RF-12RCVFB for the same pitches (Canada only). Through an open attic, regular unvented flashing is allowed. Tar the roof joint; flashing goes under the upper shingles and over the lower ones.
  7. Seal the storm collar to the chimney with silicone, then fit a Rain Cap (RM-12RRC) or Rain Cap Base (RM-12RRCB).

Height: at least 3' above the highest roof penetration and at least 2' higher than any wall, roof or building within 10' horizontally. More than 5' above the roof, secure it with a roof brace (RM-12RRB). Canada only: a flexible radiation shield tube (RM-12RRSF) wherever the chimney is enclosed, including an outside chase.
Facing & mantel

With the door and firescreen closed, cover the facing with fully non-combustible cement board at least ½" thick (HardieBacker or Durock), screwing only in the permitted areas. Finish in non-combustible materials; combustible mantels only within Tables 3 and 4.

Lintels protrude 1 ¼" past the front: ½" for the cement board and ¾" for the non-combustible finish. Heavy rock facing may need a wider custom steel lintel.

  • No gypsum board on the fireplace: it is combustible regardless of fire rating.
  • Screws allowed (grey) areas: penetrate the facing by no more than ½". With one ½" sheet of cement board, 1" screws are the maximum. No-screw (white) areas: no screws of any length or type.
  • Anything fixed over the cement board later: screws must not pass the back of the panels by more than ½". Move the firescreen and door slowly as you go to confirm nothing binds.
  • Facing finish must be non-combustible (metal, brick, slate, ceramic tile). The only combustible allowed on the facing is a mantel shelf and posts within Tables 3 and 4; televisions count as combustible.
Firebox lining

Install the chosen lining kit before the first fire: EO-VP1500 vermiculite panels (herringbone) or EO-RB1500 cement refractory bricks (running bond). Never burn without the firebox insulation and refractory bricks properly installed.

EO-VP1500 vermiculite panelssuper low emissions, very fast startup; less durable, expect wear and cracking over time
EO-RB1500 cement refractory bricksdurable, less maintenance and degradation; won't light as quickly

One of the two must be installed; each kit has its own instructions. Give both manuals to the homeowner. If the glass needs cleaning after the install, use a cleaner made for wood stove ceramic glass, never an abrasive one, and never on hot glass.

panels.title: Smoke spills into the room
items: Kitchen or bathroom fans running → negative pressure pulls smoke out; shut them off
Door opened quickly when refueling → open it slowly
Tight house → outside air helps offset depressurization, but won't stop smoking in a severely depressurized house
Exterior chimney where temperatures drop below 32°F (0°C) → poorer burning and venting, faster creosote; insulate the chase

panels.title: Signs of over-firing
items: Vermiculite panels changed color (though the Installation Manual, p. 36, calls some beige-to-orange change normal and cosmetic)
Refractory bricks cracking and deteriorating quickly
Door channel or smoke diverter warped
Causes: loads beyond about 3 logs of 22" × 6", door left partly open, more than two densified logs or more than one wax log

panels.title: Glass & door seal
items: Flames close to the glass, burning more on one side, or not burning nicely with the door closed → a gasket may need changing
Dirty glass → fire not hot enough or wood not dry enough; wax logs burned with the door closed
Door or firescreen needs significant force → something is wrong; don't force it (grease the rails each season)

panels.title: Slow to light
items: Lining has absorbed moisture after a long period without fires → first fire harder to light
Cement refractory brick lining → won't light as quickly as vermiculite
Door closed before the fire is burning briskly → poor draft and higher emissions

light.title: Building a fire
light.html:
Build the fire, and keep it, well behind the ash step refractory bricks, never against or close to the glass door or the firescreen. Use only the Renaissance andirons that came with the fireplace, and no grate. Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front.

  1. Put crumpled or loosely knotted newspaper where the kindling and logs will go.
  2. Add a generous layer of kindling over the paper, with spaces between the pieces for air.
  3. Stack 2-3 small-medium logs on the kindling, close or touching, with small gaps for air.
  4. Light the paper in a few places, then close the firescreen.
  5. Once the fire is established, add wood and close either the glass door or the firescreen. Wait to close the door until the fire is burning briskly; that gives a good draft and lower emissions.
Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or any other flammable liquid to start or refresh the fire. Keep all such liquids well away from the fireplace while it's in use.

Adding wood

Wear heavy fireplace gloves. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room. If smoke does spill, check that kitchen and bathroom fans are off.

Your first fires

Expect a little smoke and odor while oils and paint cure, so plan them for when you can open doors and windows. After a long break, the firebox lining holds moisture and the first fire may be harder to light.

door.title: The glass door & firescreen
door.html:
The glass door and the firescreen are both counterweighted and slide straight up and down.

Glass door

  • Put the handle in the door handle eye and pull up or down. The door stays wherever you stop it.
  • Run it fully open or fully closed. Never burn with it partly open: air rushes in, the burn rate goes up and the fireplace over-fires, which will permanently damage it.
  • Before closing, clear anything off the hearth threshold (the black metal surface at the bottom of the opening) so the bottom gasket can seal.
  • Don't slam it. If the glass is cracked or broken, don't burn with the door closed until the glass is replaced.

Firescreen

Lift one or both handles straight up until it clips into position. To lower it, slide the latch beside the left handle to the right and pull down.

Keep one of the two closed whenever there's a fire; never have both open. Don't touch either with bare hands while it's burning. They can be hot enough to burn you.

Burning with the glass door closed is more efficient. With it open you get more radiant heat, but heat from your home goes up the chimney. With no fire, keep the glass door closed to keep cold air out. Never step, or stand a ladder, on the metal front step.

fuel.title: What to burn
fuel.html:
Burn split, dry, seasoned wood: cut, split and stacked, covered on top but open on the sides, for at least 6 months and preferably a year or two. Wood that isn't dry won't burn cleanly or efficiently.

Is it dry enough?

Look for loose or fallen bark, cracks at the log ends, light weight compared with wood you know is dry, easy splitting, and wood that catches quickly without sizzling or dripping. A moisture meter is the best test; even an inexpensive one lets you set a standard, usually 20-25% or less.

Any well-seasoned species works. Softwoods start easily and burn quick and bright. Hardwoods take longer to season and burn longer.

Only occasionally, and carefully

  • Construction scraps (2x4 or plywood): never as your only fuel. They can overheat and seriously damage the fireplace.
  • Densified wood logs: no more than two at a time, firescreen closed.
  • Wax logs (like Duraflame): one at a time, firescreen closed. With the door closed they leave a dirty glass.
  • Use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use (in Canada they must meet ANSI/CAN/UL/ULC 2115), and read the warnings and caution markings on the package before you use them.

Don't poke or stir these while they burn. Vented gas log sets are allowed; unvented gas logs and gas lighters are not.

Never burn driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage or plastic.

load.title: How much wood to load
load.html:
There's no draft control. You set the size of the fire with the size and placement of the logs, and a couple of small logs already give big flames.

Small fire3 to 4 small logs (3" diameter)
Large fire4 to 5 small-medium logs (5" diameter)
Largest log (approx.)22" long, 6" diameter
Most at once (approx.)3 logs of that size
Maker's website: Firewood Length 24" maximum.

Lay logs on the andirons or stand them tipi-style. Tipi-style against the back is fine, but place logs carefully or you can mark the firebox bricks.

It burns clean because it's built to burn very hot, fast. Regular overloading causes durability problems and gives no benefit.

Signs you're over-firing

  • The vermiculite panels have changed color
  • The refractory bricks are cracking and deteriorating quickly
  • The door channel or the smoke diverter is warped
Note: The Owner's Manual lists vermiculite panels that have changed color as a sign of over-firing on p. 5, and the Installation Manual says some beige-to-orange color change is common with normal use and strictly cosmetic on p. 36.

Over-firing damage isn't covered by the warranty.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
A good hot fire now and then burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

Only clean it cold. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn. Never use an abrasive cleaner. Use only a cleaner your dealer recommends; wood stove glass cleaners work far better than regular glass or oven cleaners.

Open the door on its hinge

  1. Lift the firescreen all the way up and move anything on the hearth that could stop the door from opening.
  2. Close the glass door completely.
  3. Using the tip of the fireplace handle as a screwdriver, turn the two latch pins on the right of the door a quarter turn counterclockwise.
  4. Swing the door free of the guillotine frame; it swings outward from right to left. You may need to lift it slightly, but not too high, or it can bind against the firescreen.

Heat won't break the glass, but an impact can, so be careful not to hit it.

air.title: The outside air control
air.html:
If an outside air duct was installed, the fireplace uses outside air for combustion.

  • Where it is: on the left side, beyond the door rail, about halfway up. Open the glass door and the firescreen fully to reach it.
  • Down means the outside air damper is fully open. Up means fully closed.
  • It should turn freely on its pivot, so don't force it. A spring holds it open or closed; it won't move by itself.

When to use it

Renaissance recommends always using outside air when you burn with the glass door closed, and also with the firescreen closed. It can help when strong kitchen or bath fans compete with the chimney draft in a tightly built house, but it won't stop smoking in a severely depressurized house.

Close it when the fireplace isn't burning, to keep cold air out.

The control and the parts around it can be hot enough to cause serious burns. Use a gloved hand to adjust it when the fireplace is hot.

ash.title: Ashes & everyday cleaning
ash.html:
Take the ashes out before they get deep enough to spill over the ash step refractory bricks.

  1. Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  2. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until final disposal.
  3. If you'll bury or spread the ashes, keep them in the closed container until every cinder is completely out.
Hot coals buried in ashes can stay very hot for a long time.

Wiping it down

Clean any black painted part of the fireplace with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water. Don't use abrasive cleaners.

Touching up the paint

Metal areas on the face can be touched up with Stove Bright Metallic Black high temperature paint, sold at most fireplace dealers. Never paint it while it's still warm, keep the spray can away from heat and flame, keep the room ventilated until the paint is dry, and cover the glass, surround and hearth extension first.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
When wood burns slowly, it gives off tar and vapors that mix with moisture from the wood and condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot chimney fire.

A fireplace as clean burning as this one shouldn't make much creosote. Still:

  • Have the chimney inspected for creosote after a couple of months of use. How fast it builds up tells you how often to check.
  • Have it inspected at least once a year.
  • A buildup of 1/8" (3mm) or more calls for immediate cleaning by a chimney professional, and possibly a change in how you burn and more frequent checks.
  • Depending on how you burn, expect cleaning every year or every other year.
The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass, and the cleaner the chimney.

care.title: Season-start care
care.html:
Grease the door rails

At the start of every burning season:

  1. Open the firescreen and the glass door completely.
  2. Put a small amount of the high temperature grease that came with the fireplace on each guide rail, left and right, just below the bottom of the door.
  3. Move the door up and down a couple of times to spread the grease along the rails. Repeat for the firescreen.
Regular grease can't take the heat. Don't use Teflon-based or silicone-based products such as Jig-A-Loo: burned Teflon can release a toxic fume. Your Renaissance dealer sells more high temperature grease.

The door and firescreen shouldn't need much force. If you have to push hard, something is wrong; stop, or you could damage or break something.

Keep an eye on the gaskets

Several gaskets seal the door so the air wash can keep the glass clean. If, with the door closed, the flames come close to the glass, burn more on one side, or just don't burn nicely, a gasket may need changing. The bottom stainless-steel gasket lasts longer if you keep the hearth threshold clean. The gasket on the back of the glass door needs changing every few years, depending on how often you swing the door open.

warranty.title: 30-year limited warranty
warranty.html:
All Renaissance Fireplaces models are warranted against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, in three stages:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Second through fifth yearsDefective parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Sixth through thirtieth yearsReplacement parts, if available, at 50% of the published retail price; no labor

Not covered

  • Glass and andirons
  • Normal wear and tear, such as paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked rigid insulation panels or firebox lining parts
  • Damage from vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or not servicing the unit
  • Repairs not authorized in advance, especially travel and labor charges

Defective parts are returned to an authorized Renaissance Fireplaces dealer, and freight for replacement parts isn't covered. The warranty isn't transferable, doesn't cover damage in transit, and doesn't apply if the installation doesn't follow the installation and owner's manuals.

This is a summary. The full terms and limitations are in the manual.

specEmis.title: Emissions, burn rate & weight
specEmis.html:
Lined with the optional vermiculite panels (EO-VP1500), it has met the EPA Voluntary Wood Burning Fireplace Program Phase 2 emission level, with these figures:

Door open, firescreen closed3.4 g/kg
Door closed0.68 g/kg
Door closed, equivalent3.95 g/hr
Typical burn rate5.9 kg/hr

Emission rates per the ASTM 2558 test protocol.

Weight, crated970 lb
Maker's website: Shipping weight 851 lbs.

Under the 2015 U.S. EPA regulation it is defined as a fireplace (more than 500 square inches of fire viewing).

Maker's website: EPA status: The Rumford 1500 can be sold in Canada and the USA since it is not regulated as per the rule definition of 'fireplace' under Subpart AAA of the 2015 EPA Standards of Performance for New Residential Wood Heaters Vol. 80, No. 50.

Built-in guillotine glass door and guillotine firescreen. Floor reinforcement may be required; keep it on its skid until ready to install. Designed for wood logs; can be converted to vented gas log sets. No unvented gas log sets, gas log lighters, or wood or gas fireplace inserts.

Note: For the viewing area, the Installation Manual describes approximately 1500 square inches of viewing space on p. 2 and gives 1360 square visible inches of pure fire viewing on p. 8 (the Owner's Manual also gives 1360 on p. 6).
Maker's website: Glass Size 1450 in².

Note: The Table 6 elevation bands overlap: the manual's first row reads 0 - 1500 ft and the next row starts at 1001 ft, both on p. 28, so 1001 to 1500 ft falls in two rows with different flue heights.

specClear.html:

The remaining framing dimensions are shown only on the Figure 3 drawing on this page, and the fireplace dimensions only on Figure 2 (p. 9).

index_extra.p: Inspect after a couple of months, then at least yearly
Open the door slowly; turn off kitchen and bath fans
Wax logs one at a time, firescreen closed
Vented sets permitted; unvented gas logs and gas lighters are not
Grease the guide rails every burning season
Oils and paint curing; open doors and windows
RM-12RTS mandatory; bracket position per Table 9

conflicts.issue: Owner's Manual lists 'vermiculite panels have changed color' as a sign of over-firing; Installation Manual says some beige-to-orange color change of the vermiculite is common with normal use, permanent but strictly cosmetic.
Viewing area: 'approximately 1500 square inches of beautiful viewing space' (install p. 2) vs '1360 square visible inches' (install p. 8; owner's p. 6).

Table 6 (recommended minimum flue height): first elevation band printed '0 - 1500' while the next band is '1001 - 2000', so 1001-1500 ft falls in two rows with different heights. Table not transcribed.

Vented flashing part: the text says 'A vented flashing (RF-12RVF) MUST be used if the chimney is in a chase or is enclosed to the roof'; Table 9 on the same page lists vented flashing under 'US only' (RF-12RVF, RF-12RVFA, RF-12RVFB) and 'Canada only' (RF-12RCVF, RF-12RCVFA, RF-12RCVFB), by roof pitch.
conflicts.reason: The text names one vented flashing part; Table 9 gives the part by roof pitch and country. Both fit, and the step now names both. The pitch range for each part is not transcribed: the table text doesn't show it unambiguously.

catalog_mismatches.manual: Approximate maximum log size 22" in length, 6" in diameter (over-firing guidelines; also 'overall length equivalent to 22"' on p. 4)

catalog_mismatches.catalog: qualifies at EPA Voluntary Fireplace Program Phase 2 level (no lining condition)
catalog_mismatches.manual: Met the EPA Voluntary Wood Burning Fireplace Program Phase 2 emission level 'when lined with the optional vermiculite panels'; not stated for the cement refractory brick lining (EO-RB1500)
Weight when crated is 970 lb (also 'weighs 970 lb crated' on p. 14); the website labels its figure 'Shipping weight'
No glass size as such; 'approximately 1500 square inches of beautiful viewing space' (p. 2) and '1360 square visible inches' of pure fire viewing (p. 8; Owner's Manual p. 6)
No outside dimensions in the text; shown only on the Figure 2 Fireplace Dimensions drawing (install p. 9)

review.notes: No listing/certification standard is named in either manual (the listing label is on the left counterweight channel but its text is not reproduced), so shell.certification is omitted; the manuals give no model number beyond the document code RR1500C. Content shown only as drawings or hard-to-read tables was not transcribed: fireplace dimensions (Fig. 2, install p. 9), framing layout (Fig. 3, p. 10; only the 94" / 88 3/4" framing heights are in text), clearance drawing (Fig. 10, p. 22), hearth figures (p. 26), anti-tip bracket options (Fig. 9, p. 21), permissible screw areas (Fig. 16, p. 35), Table 6 flue heights (p. 28), Table 7 RIS offsets (p. 29) and Table 9 roof top shield bracket positions (p. 33). Through-the-wall values shown are the 30-degree (US and Canada) column of Table 8 (p. 30). Catalog height/width/depth (87.75 / 59.125 / 32.5 in) cannot be checked (Fig. 2 only). Catalog weight 851 lb is not comparable: the manual gives only 970 lb crated (install pp. 8, 14). Catalog glass_area 1450 sq in is not stated in the manual. Part numbers for the Insulated Angled Wall Radiation Shield are printed with different letter order, 'RM-12WRSI30 or RM-12RWSI45' (p. 29); reproduced as printed, confirm with ICC. Table 5 text reads 'USG Micore 1604' and 'USG Micore 3004' where the trailing 4 is the footnote marker; the guide writes Micore 160 / Micore 300 (the manual's own worked example says 'Micore 300'). There is no troubleshooting chart; fault panels are built from the owner's manual's fault descriptions (smoke spillage, over-firing signs, gasket symptoms, first-fire moisture). Every install-manual page carries a stray template line 'ERROR! USE THE HOME TAB...'; no content appears to be missing.
